StateDispatcher.discribe: StateDispatcher is an abstract base class for building strongly typed state managers outside of React. It solves one problem: providing subclasses with a convenient and strictly typed API for declaring state, mutating it through setters, and subscribing via {EventEmitter}.
StateDispatcher.discribe_2: Unlike Redux or Zustand, StateDispatcher is not a global store. It is a foundation for creating isolated classes with their own logic—a localization manager, authentication manager, form manager, and so on. Each class is a self-contained object where all state mutations happen internally, while only a strongly typed API is exposed externally.

concept.title: Concept
concept.desc: StateDispatcher is parameterized with two generics:
concept.state: the state shape — the complete object stored inside the manager
concept.events: Record<string, any> — a dictionary of events: key → value type received by subscribers
concept.abt: {StateValues} and {Events} do not have to match. The state may contain more fields than are exposed through Events, or a setter may transform the input value and emit a completely different type. See the {Setters} section for details.
concept.ex_bornYear: computed field, has no dedicated setter

initial.title: Initialization
initial.desc: To create your own manager, simply extend {StateDispatcher} and pass the initial state and setters object to {super}:

arguments.title: Constructor Arguments
arguments.initialState: StateValues — the initial state; stored and mutated in place
arguments.setters: SetterMap<State, Events> — an object where each Events key has a corresponding mutator function
arguments.maxListeners: number? — maximum number of listeners per event (defaults to EventEmitter's standard limit of 10)

setters.title: setters
setters.desc: A public setter {setter} is automatically generated for every key in {Events}. When called, it passes {state} and {value} to the corresponding mutator function, updates the state, and then emits an event to all subscribers.
setters.desc_2: If the mutator function returns a value, subscribers receive that value. If nothing is returned ({undefined}), subscribers receive the original {value}. This allows the emitted data to have a different shape from the stored state:
setters.with_return: returns a value → subscribers receive an object

listen.desc: {ex} subscribes to a specific event and returns an unsubscribe function. The callback receives the value emitted by the corresponding setter (including any transformation).

getState.desc: {getState} returns {state} — a snapshot of the current state. {readonly} guarantees that nobody outside the manager can mutate the state directly; it can only be modified through setters.
getState.desc_2: Inside a subclass, {getState} is convenient for reading the current state between operations.

destroyDispatcher.desc: {destroyDispatcher} is a protected method that removes all listeners and marks the manager as destroyed using the {isDestroyed} flag. To expose it publicly, the subclass must explicitly decide whether and how to do so.
destroyDispatcher.react: A typical pattern in a React component:

createHook.desc: {createHook} is a helper utility for React that eliminates repetitive subscription and cleanup boilerplate. It accepts a manager and returns a hook factory that makes subscribing to individual state fields convenient.
createHook.key: event key from the Events map
createHook.selector: selector: specifies which field to read and return from StateValues
createHook.arg_1: keyof Events — the event key the hook subscribes to
createHook.arg_2: (state: StateValues) => Events[K] — extracts the current value from the state during initialization and after every emit
createHook.unmount: The subscription is automatically removed when the component unmounts.

limits.title: Limitations
limits.abstract: Abstract class — cannot be instantiated directly
limits.disc: StateDispatcher is {abstract}. It is not intended to be used directly and always requires a subclass. This is a deliberate design decision: the subclass defines the domain, public API, and lifecycle.
limits.mutate_desc: State is mutated in place inside setter functions. There is no immutability, diffing, or structural sharing. These features are intentionally excluded from StateDispatcher because they do not align with its philosophy.
limits.middleware_desc: There is no built-in time travel, devtools, middleware chains, or transactions. Each setter is a simple atomic operation.

typo.title: Type Safety
typo.desc: Across many projects I've worked on, route typing was surprisingly often a source of problems.
typo.desc_2: In most cases, there was no route typing at all. I had to manually search for links to the required pages. On top of that, simple typos could make a page either inaccessible or effectively hidden.
typo.desc_3: PathRouter provides strict route typing, making navigation more convenient through autocompletion while also improving safety, since incorrect or misspelled paths are caught at compile time.

modals.title: Modal Windows
modals.desc: In many React applications, modal windows are not part of the navigation and are instead controlled by {state}. As a result, the modal state is not reflected in the URL, meaning users cannot bookmark an opened modal or expect it to reopen after refreshing the page.
modals.desc_2: A simple example is a wallet modal. Opening it may seem perfectly natural from a UI perspective, yet there will always be users who prefer the site to open directly with their account balance displayed.
modals.desc_3: PathRouter treats a modal window as part of the URL while keeping the resulting URL clean and easy to understand:

features.title: Features
features.desc_2: All you need to define are the route keys in the configuration object. Instead of repeating the same keys over and over:
features.desc_3: PathRouter simplifies this into a convenient tree structure:

typo_nav.title: Strongly Typed Navigation
typo_nav.desc: PathRouter solves what has always been my biggest issue with routing systems: the lack of TypeScript autocompletion in conventional routing implementations.
typo_nav.desc_2: It's surprisingly common to dig through files or components just to find the correct route.
typo_nav.desc_3: Thanks to autocompletion, PathRouter always suggests every available route defined in your project.

url_modal.title: URL-Driven Modals
url_modal.desc: PathRouter uses the URL as the single source of truth for determining whether a modal is open and what parameters it contains. It also provides a simple and intuitive API for working with them:

install.title: Installation
install.desc: To use PathRouter, install it from npm:

init.title: Initialization
init.desc: For both type safety and runtime safety, PathRouter is created through a factory that accepts a {route-config}.
init.desc_2: The configuration is divided into two sections: pages and modals. Modals remain a flat list, while pages can be nested arbitrarily.
init.desc_3: A simple example of creating a PathRouter:

router-tree.title: Router Tree
router-tree.desc: The core feature of PathRouter is its support for deeply nested page hierarchies.
router-tree.desc_2: This hierarchy is built using the {setPage} function. It constructs and configures the routing tree for further use by the router.
router-tree.desc_3: From there, all that's left is to place it into the configuration object at the desired nesting level:
router-tree.desc_4: The internal {parseRouteConfig} function produces a parsed configuration object containing the full path and metadata for every page. This information can be used, for example, to generate a sitemap or for debugging purposes.
router-tree.desc_5: Now let's take a look at the routes PathRouter generates from our configuration object:
router-tree.desc_6: This makes it easy to change routes, add new ones, and expand the navigation tree without manually rewriting paths.

sitemap.text: For example, you can view this site's sitemap {hereLink}, generated using the very same approach.

pagesContainer.desc: {PagesContainer} is the component responsible for rendering all pages and modal windows.
pagesContainer.desc_2: Internally, it wraps {Routes} from react-router-dom and renders an internal {ModalsContainer} only when a modal is currently present in the URL.
pagesContainer.desc_3: The position of {PagesContainer} within your component tree determines where both the page content and modal content will be rendered.

fallback.desc: The {fallback} prop is passed to the internal {suspense} component and is displayed while lazy-loaded ({lazy}) pages and modals are loading. Defaults to {null}.

modalWrapper.desc: {ModalWrapper} is an optional wrapper component for modal content. If omitted, the modal is rendered directly into the DOM without any container or animation. If provided, PathRouter renders the active modal component inside it and passes the following props:
modalWrapper.modalName: The current modal key (the first segment after /modal/)
modalWrapper.isOpen: Whether a modal is currently open
modalWrapper.onClose: Closes the modal through the router (updates the URL)
modalWrapper.children: The modal component from the configuration, already wrapped in {Suspense}
modalWrapper.ref: PathRouter also reads a forwarded ref exposing the {handleCloseWithAnimation} method. If present, the router calls this method before updating the URL, allowing the component to finish its closing animation before the navigation occurs.
modalWrapper.animation_comment: play the animation, then close the modal

getPath.desc: {getPath} and {getModal} are identity functions: they simply return the argument unchanged. Their sole purpose is TypeScript type narrowing. The compiler verifies that the provided string is a valid route or modal key defined in your configuration and reports a compile-time error if it isn't.
getPath.desc_2: They're useful anywhere {usePath} or {NavLink} isn't available—for example, in menu configurations, data arrays, or utility functions:
getPath.compile_error: compile-time error if "profile" does not exist

navLink.desc: {NavLink} is a router-aware replacement for the {a} tag. It renders a real {href} (so right-click → "Open in New Tab", SSR, and search engine crawlers all work correctly), while intercepting the primary left-click and invoking {pageNavigate} within the SPA—without reloading the page.
navLink.desc_2: Clicks with modifier keys (Cmd / Ctrl / Shift / Alt) or with a {target} attribute other than {self} are ignored, allowing the browser to handle them normally.
navLink.to: Navigation target. If omitted, the current page is preserved
navLink.modal: The modal to open after navigation
navLink.modalBreadCrumbs: Additional URL segments appended after the modal name
navLink.replace: Replaces the current history entry instead of creating a new one
navLink.navigateOptions: Additional options passed to react-router's navigate function
navLink.activeClassName: CSS class applied to the <a> element when the link is active

active.title: Active State
active.desc: NavLink is considered active when {pagePath} matches {to}. If {modal} is specified, {modalName} must also match the provided key. Active links automatically receive the {ariaCurrent} and {dataActive} attributes.

examples.open_modal: Open a modal without changing the current page
examples.navigate_and_open_modal: Navigate to another page and open a modal at the same time
examples.replace_history: Replace the current history entry (no "Back" button)

usePath.desc: {usePath} is a hook that returns the entire router state, fully typed according to your configuration. It is available in any component rendered below {PathProvider}.
usePath.pagePath: The current page path (excluding the /modal/... segment)
usePath.pageIsHavePrevHistory: false if the page was opened directly (there is no previous history entry)
usePath.back_button_condition: show the "Back" button only if a previous page exists
usePath.modalIsOpen: Whether any modal is currently open
usePath.modalName: The key of the currently open modal (the first segment after /modal/)
usePath.modalPath: The full modal path including breadcrumbs, for example "wallet/balance"
usePath.modalBreadCrumbs: Additional segments following the modal name
usePath.modalClose: Closes the modal and returns to the current page

searchParams.desc: PathRouter provides a complete API for working with query string parameters. All values are stored as a {record}, where every key always contains an array—even if only a single value is provided. This makes working with multiple values for the same parameter (for example, {tag}) straightforward.
searchParams.params: A reactive snapshot of the current query parameters
searchParams.change: merge: string → sets a single value, array → appends values to the existing ones. Other keys remain unchanged
searchParams.set: replace: completely replaces the value of the specified key without affecting any other keys
searchParams.footer: All operations preserve the current URL (pathname, the /modal/... segment, and the hash). Only the query string is modified.
searchParams.change_merge: change — merge: new values are appended to the existing ones
searchParams.set_replace: set — replace: completely replaces only this key while leaving all others untouched

redirects.title: Redirects
redirects.desc: To redirect users to another route, pass {redirect} to {setPage} instead of a component. PathRouter will internally use {navigate} from react-router-dom. Redirects are most commonly used together with the {catchAll} wildcard to handle unknown nested routes:

limits.title: Limitations
limits.desc: PathRouter is designed to solve its problem well, but it isn't the right fit for every use case:

browserRouter.title: BrowserRouter Only / CSR Only
browserRouter.desc: {PathProvider} internally uses {BrowserRouter} from react-router-dom. As a result, HashRouter is not supported, and server-side rendering frameworks (such as Next.js or Remix), where routing is managed by the framework itself, are not compatible.

modalSegment.title: Reserved {modalSegment} Segment
modalSegment.desc: PathRouter distinguishes between pages and modals by splitting the URL at the {modalSegment} delimiter. No page route should contain this segment in its path, as it will be interpreted as the start of a modal route.

flatModals.title: Flat Modals — One at a Time
flatModals.desc: The {modals} section of the configuration is a flat dictionary. Nested modals and displaying multiple modals simultaneously are not supported. Navigation within a modal should be implemented using {modalBreadCrumbs} rather than opening another modal on top of the current one.

animation.title: Animations via ModalWrapper Only
animation.desc: PathRouter does not include built-in animations. Modals appear and disappear instantly. To support animated transitions, implement your own {ModalWrapper} exposing the {handleCloseWithAnimation} method.

depth.title: Maximum Nesting Depth: 8 Levels
depth.desc: TypeScript's type recursion used by {PageEntries} is limited to eight levels of route nesting. Projects with deeper hierarchies will still compile successfully, but autocompletion for deeply nested routes may become unreliable.

Home.title: A Catalog of Engineering Solutions
Home.description: Modules, architectural patterns, and optimizations built for real-world problems.
Home.abt: Each case study includes an implementation, API reference, and an explanation of the design decisions.

PathRouter.desc: A React routing engine where the URL is the single source of truth.
PathRouter.desc_2: Provides route autocompletion, nested routing, and type-safe navigation.

StateDispatcher.desc: A base class for building isolated, strongly typed state managers.
StateDispatcher.desc_2: Combines encapsulated state, controlled state transformations, and EventEmitter-based subscriptions.
